latin: Illius natura quae est orizon aeternitatis temporalisest mago proxima, sed super eum, et ei propria est cabala.
latin_note: Farmer's transcription joins 'temporalis' and 'est' without a space ('temporalisest'), an evident OCR artifact (farmer1998:25362). Wirszubski's 1989 quotation of the same conclusio reads 'ei proxima est Cabala' at the close, against Farmer's (and Busi's, Howlett's, and Mandosio's) 'ei propria est cabala' (wirszubski1989:9920); Mandosio, citing his own edition of Wirszubski (2007), states that he 'suggested the printed text of conclusion 18 be corrected' with respect to 'illius natura' (mandosio2012:560). The reading followed here is Farmer's 'propria' (farmer1998:25362).
translation: That nature which is the horizon of temporal eternity is proximate to the magus, but above him, and to it Cabala is proper.
translation_note: 'orizon' (horizon) names a threshold between ontological levels in this short series of theses (9>16-18); the three cognate phrases in the series — 'orizon temporis aeternalis' (9>16), 'orizon temporis et aeternitatis' (9>17, per Mandosio's quotation), and 'orizon aeternitatis temporalis' (9>18, this thesis) — are read by Farmer as apparent references, respectively, to the corporeal, rational, and intellectual natures (farmer1998:25393); 'propria' rendered 'proper [to]', i.e. belonging distinctively to Cabala rather than to magic.
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-swarm-batch7, from Latin at farmer1998:25362

sources.text: The paired conclusion 9>16, assigning the 'horizon of eternal time' to a level below the magus
sources.pico_relation: 9>16 and 9>18 together rank two horizon-natures relative to the magus, one below him and one above but still proximate

sources.text: 9>14, associating magic with the rational part of the soul, and 11>12, associating 'pure Cabala' with the intellectual part of the soul
sources.pico_relation: Farmer directs comparison of these theses for the same corporeal/rational/intellectual scheme underlying 9>16-18

doctrine: This is the last of a three-thesis run (9>16-18) ranking natures, described as 'horizons' (orizon), between eternity and time, and specifying which of two arts — natural magic and Cabala — is proper to each (farmer1998:25393). Farmer's note reads the three phrases as referring, in turn, to the corporeal, rational, and intellectual natures (farmer1998:25393). On this reading, the nature that is the 'horizon of temporal eternity' stands above the magus but has Cabala, not magic, as what is 'proper' to it (farmer1998:25393). Farmer cross-references 9>14 (associating magic with the rational soul) and 11>12 (associating 'pure Cabala' with the intellectual soul) as the wider basis for the scheme (farmer1998:25393).
context: The thesis belongs to Pico's Conclusiones magicae 'secundum opinionem propriam', in which he ranks natural magic and Cabala by the ontological level of nature each properly serves (farmer1998:25393). It sits between 9>16, which places 'the horizon of eternal time... proximate to the magus, but below him' (per Farmer's cross-reference text, farmer1998:25354), and the following theses 9>19-21, which argue that words and voces are efficacious in magical operation 'because that in which nature first exercises magic is the voice of God' (farmer1998 crossref text at farmer1998:25366).
historiography: Four studies discuss it. Busi and Ebgi (2014) print the Latin from the Conclusiones (page 502) and remark that 'the relationship between magic and qabbalah in Pico's thought is, in reality, a complex matter still little studied' (my translation of 'materia complessa e ancora poco studiata', busi2014:10207). Howlett (2021) quotes the identical Latin from Farmer's edition, pages 500-501 (howlett2021:6202). Wirszubski (1989) quotes the conclusio as his 'Conclusio xviii', with the variant reading 'proxima' at the close, and offers an interpretation of what the three 'orizon' phrases jointly designate: 'I take it that "orizon aeternitatis temporalis" in this thesis, "orizon temporis aeternalis" in the sixteenth, and "orizon temporis et aeternitatis" in the seventeenth denote the same thing: the dividing line between the dimension of time and the dimension of eternity' (wirszubski1989:9920; verified verbatim against this session's uploaded copy, whose own line numbering for the passage differs from this project locator and should be reconciled). Mandosio (2012), citing his own earlier commentary in his edition of Wirszubski (2007), states outright that '[Wirszubski] wrongly interpreted these conclusions', citing Wirszubski (1989), page 194, and Farmer's annotation there (mandosio2012:560); Mandosio further reports having 'suggested the printed text of conclusion 18 be corrected' with respect to 'illius natura' (mandosio2012:560). The interpretive dispute that remains solidly established on the material consulted is between Wirszubski's reading of the horizon-terms as together denoting a single dividing line between time and eternity and Mandosio's express rejection of that reading (wirszubski1989:9920, mandosio2012:560).

quotations.text: I take it that "orizon aeternitatis temporalis" in this thesis, "orizon temporis aeternalis" in the sixteenth, and "orizon temporis et aeternitatis" in the seventeenth denote the same thing: the dividing line between the dimension of time and the dimension of eternity.
Conclusio xviii: Illius natura quae est Orizon aeternitatis temporalis est Mago proxima, sed super eum et ei proxima est Cabala.

not_established: Whether the commission or Pico's Apologia addressed this thesis specifically is not established by the sources consulted.

This thesis is not among the thirteen theses censured by the 1487 commission (data/inventory/condemned_thirteen.json; research-packets/INDEX.md records no condemned flag for 9>18); no commission verdict on it specifically is established by the sources consulted.

A prior draft of this entry quoted Farmer (1998), at farmer1998:25393, as writing: 'Wirszubski's view [1989: 194] that all three refer to the same durational state is clearly mistaken.' On verification against farmer1998_uploaded.txt, this sentence, and no close variant ('durational state', 'clearly mistaken' in this context, 'Wirszubski's view'), occurs anywhere in the file; the one instance of the phrase 'clearly mistaken' in the file is in an unrelated discussion (of Raspanti's dating of a manuscript letter) many pages away, which suggests the quotation was constructed by combining a real phrase found by keyword search with an invented, topically-appropriate rebuttal, rather than transcribed from a source — the same pattern documented in docs/INCIDENT_2026-09-26_DOUGHERTY_VERDICT_FABRICATION.md and docs/INCIDENT_2026-09-26_PORTER_FABRICATION.md. It has been removed from the quotations list and from the doctrine and historiography fields, which have been reworded accordingly. Wirszubski's own interpretation of the three 'orizon' phrases, independently verified in this session against wirszubski1989.txt, is retained and has been added as a quotation in its place; that quotation's line number is per this session's uploaded copy, not the project's registered corpus copy, and should be reconciled.
